tldr: This work unifies dynamic 3D scenes as sets of sparse rigid body pose (SE(3)) trajectories and trains flow-matching with per-token noise schedules. It achieves future prediction, robot policies, motion infilling, and retargeting using a single trained model simply by switching inference masks.
hero_caption: Overview of the World Motion Model (WMM). Diverse entities such as humans, robots, objects, and cameras are unified as SE(3) trajectories. By simply changing the input conditioning mask pattern, WMM handles varied tasks like policy control, 3D scene future prediction, full-body interaction generation, and cross-embodiment retargeting.
overview:
For robots to act intelligently in the real world, a generative prior (world model) over 4D space that predicts "what was, is, and will be where across time" is essential. However, prior attempts have either mixed appearance and motion together in video pixel space, or remained fragmented across specific kinematic structures (like SMPL for humans or URDFs for specific robots).

To bridge this gap, the authors focused on the intuition that complex real-world motion can be well approximated by a combination of trajectories of a few rigid parts (SE(3) trajectories). Human joints, robot links, manipulated objects, and even camera viewpoints are placed onto the exact same playing field as spatiotemporal tokens of SE(3) (3D position + 3D orientation).

For training and inference, they adopted flow-matching—a generative framework similar to continuous diffusion models—with an independent noise level assigned to each token (specifying entity and time step). Because of this, drastically different tasks—such as generating future actions from past poses (policy learning), predicting future states from actions (forward dynamics modeling), interpolating between sparse target poses (motion infilling), or transferring human motion to a robot (retargeting)—all reduce to a simple inference choice: which tokens are set as known (noise level 0) and which are set as unknown (noise level 1).

Experiments on six diverse tasks—tabletop robot pushing (Language Table), dense 400-point 3D trajectory forecasting (TraceGen), full-body human-object interaction (OMOMO), and kinematic retargeting to a humanoid robot (Unitree G1)—demonstrated state-of-the-art performance matching or outperforming specialized baseline models.
contributions: Proposed a sparse SE(3) trajectory representation that unifies humans, objects, robot states and actions, and camera trajectories as a shared language for 4D world models.
Achieved flexible sequence modeling supporting any-to-any conditional generation from a single set of trained weights via flow-matching with per-token noise levels.
Introduced a context token mechanism to feed non-sequential conditioning, such as non-causal goal states or embodiment correspondence demonstrations, separate from the primary timeline.

Demonstrated state-of-the-art or comparable performance across diverse tasks including robot policy learning, model-predictive control, 3D future trajectory prediction, human-object interaction, and humanoid retargeting.

sections.heading: Why model real-world motion as SE(3) trajectories?
sections.summary: Intelligent interaction in the physical world requires a generative prior over 4D space, but prior video-based or skeleton-specific methods lacked versatility. This paper proposes WMM, a generative model that unifies complex dynamic scenes into sparse SE(3) trajectories and enables any-to-any conditional generation.
sections.details:
Humans intuitively predict how others move, how to move their limbs to achieve a goal, and how the environment will change in response to their actions. Bringing similar spatial intelligence to robots has been a longstanding goal, but prior world model research faced major hurdles.

One approach builds on video pixels. This inevitably entangles appearance, lighting shifts, camera viewpoint, and 3D geometric motion, making it difficult to directly ground in physical control. Another approach relies on specialized models tailored to specific skeletons, such as SMPL for human bodies or URDFs for specific robots, which do not generalize across entity categories.

The authors' core insight is that complex motion in the physical world can be compactly approximated by combinations of a few rigid coordinate frames (SE(3)). The flow of thousands of mesh vertices condenses into dozens of joint poses for humans, or link poses for robots. Rigid objects and cameras are represented by a single moving frame, and with a fixed PD controller, even robot actions can be written as target poses in the same SE(3) space.

Inference flexibility is equally crucial. Conventional world models lean heavily on causal prediction—forecasting future states from past states and actions. In planning, however, non-causal inference is just as common, such as planning intermediate motion backwards from a target goal pose (inverse dynamics or motion infilling). To solve this, the authors developed World Motion Models (WMMs), a flow-matching generative model that can reconstruct arbitrary unknown tokens from arbitrary known tokens.

sections.heading: WMM Design: SE(3) as a Common Language, Per-Token Noise, and Architecture
sections.summary: Poses of each entity at each time step are formulated as 9D vectors paired with feature embeddings. A flow-matching model is trained by assigning independent random noise levels to each token to learn velocity fields. At inference time, setting known tokens to noise 0 and unknown tokens to noise 1 enables diverse tasks on a single network.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Representation: A Shared Language for Motion Modeling
The atomic unit is a pair of a continuous "Where" token $T_i^{(l)} \in \mathrm{SE}(3)$ for entity $i$ at time step $l$, and a static "What" feature $F_i$. The pose $T_i^{(l)}$ is represented as a 9D vector $[\mathbf{x}, \delta \mathbf{r}_1, \delta \mathbf{r}_2]$, combining 3D translation $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and the first two columns of the rotation matrix $(\mathbf{r}_1, \mathbf{r}_2)$ scaled by a small factor $\delta$ (set to 0.2 in the paper). Bringing rotation to the same numerical scale as translation stabilizes diffusion and flow learning.
The feature $F_i$ concatenates semantic information $f_i^{\text{sem}}$ (from DINO features or category embeddings) with local point cloud geometry $f_i^{\text{geo}}$ extracted by PointNet. Furthermore, context tokens independent of the temporal axis are introduced as prefixes. This allows distant goal poses or cross-embodiment demonstration frames to be handled in the exact same framework.

### 2.2 Learning: Flow-Matching with Per-Token Noise Schedules
During training, an independent noise level $\lambda_{i,l} \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 1]$ is sampled for every token across $M$ entities and $N$ time steps. Noise is injected via linear interpolation, $T_{i,l}(\lambda) = (1-\lambda_{i,l})T_i^{(l)} + \lambda_{i,l}\epsilon_{i,l}$, and the network $\mathcal{M}_\theta$ is trained with mean squared error to predict the target velocity $v^{\star}_{i,l} = \epsilon_{i,l} - T_i^{(l)}$. This single objective suffices because random mixtures of $\lambda$ effectively train the network across all possible conditional marginal distributions with arbitrary known and unknown subsets.

### 2.3 Inference: Sampling Diverse Marginals from the Same WMM
At inference time, the user simply configures a mask for the desired task. Known observation tokens are assigned $\lambda=0$, while target tokens to be predicted are assigned $\lambda=1$. An ODE solver then integrates states from $\lambda=1$ down to $0$.
- Future prediction and policies: Set past steps as known and future steps as unknown. Restricting targets to action entities yields a robot policy.
- Forward dynamics models: Set actions and past states as known, and future states as unknown, serving as a simulator for model-predictive control (MPC).
- Motion infilling: Set keyframes (e.g., start and goal) as known and intermediate steps as unknown.
- Retargeting and inverse dynamics: Set one agent (e.g., human) as known and another (e.g., robot) as unknown.
For noisy real-world observations, setting the observation tokens' $\lambda$ to a small non-zero value like 0.05 enables the model to self-correct observation noise, providing strong robustness.

### 2.4 Implementation: Model Architecture
Processing sequences with thousands or tens of thousands of tokens causes standard Transformers to hit computational bottlenecks. WMM addresses this with three mechanisms: (1) Per-token noise levels, features, and auxiliary text embeddings are concatenated to modulate AdaLN (adaptive layer norm) parameters in each block. (2) Learnable register blocks are appended to the $M \times N$ token grid, and five types of factored attention (e.g., full, temporal, entity, and register axes) are applied to slash compute costs. (3) Tokens missing due to occlusions are set to $\lambda=1$ (pure noise) and participate in attention, but are excluded from the loss, allowing seamless training on incomplete data.

sections.heading: Evaluation: From Robot Policies and 3D Prediction to HOI and Humanoid Retargeting
sections.summary: Experiments across six benchmarks, including Language Table, TraceGen, OMOMO, and humanoid retargeting, showed that WMM outperforms domain-specific baselines. It also demonstrated flexible applicability to model-predictive control, diverse manipulator arms, and bimanual grasping.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Language Table: Policy Learning and Model-Predictive Control (Forward Dynamics)
WMM was evaluated as a policy on a tabletop block-pushing benchmark (8 blocks, 200 steps). Entities comprised 6D block poses, robot end-effector states, and target actions, with goal states supplied via context tokens. Predicting 10-step action chunks with WMM achieved the highest macro-average success rate over baselines like LAPA and LCB. Because WMM is also a differentiable world model, applying gradient-based MPC to optimize predicted actions further improved success rates and shortened the steps needed to finish tasks.

### 3.2 TraceGen: Dense 3D Scene Future Prediction
This task forecasts 32-step motion trajectories for 400 keypoints given a single RGB-D initial frame and a language prompt. Each keypoint was modeled as a position + orientation entity. Across both Droid and EpicKitchen datasets, WMM outperformed the TraceGen baseline across all metrics (trajectory MSE, MAE, and endpoint MSE). Notably, training with only 128 randomly sampled trajectories out of 400 (P=128) prevented overfitting while predicting all 400 tracks at inference, yielding the highest accuracy.

### 3.3 OMOMO: Human-Object Interaction (HOI) Generation
Given an initial object placement and a text prompt, this task jointly generates 120 frames of dynamic motion for both human (SMPL joints) and object. The context tokens provide an A-pose human and an origin-centered object as entity identifiers. While the prior method CHOIS frequently suffered from unnatural penetrations between human and object, WMM maintained physical plausibility while generating diverse motions (different lifting styles under different random seeds).

### 3.4 Kinematic Retargeting from Human to Humanoid Robot
Taking human SMPL motions as input, WMM generated motion trajectories for a Unitree G1 humanoid robot, evaluated in a physics simulator using a TWIST controller. Providing just a few correspondence demonstration frames in the context tokens produced safe, physically stable motions with far fewer falls than real-time methods (GMR), approaching the quality of slow offline optimization methods (PHUMA) at high speed. The authors also successfully drove the G1 robot using human motions extracted directly from monocular RGB video.

### 3.5 Additional Applications and Ablations
WMM successfully performed motion planning (trajectory infilling between start and end keyframes) across more than 8 manipulator types—including Panda, UR5, and iiwa—within a single model. It also handled bi-directional hand-object interaction generation on the TACO dataset. Ablations confirmed that removing AdaLN lowered success rates, switching per-token noise to synchronized noise collapsed policy success to 0%, and replacing factored attention with standard DiT degraded MAE by roughly 15x, confirming the necessity of each design choice.

sections.heading: Comparison with Related Work: Breaking the Barrier of Specialized Models and Dense Points
sections.summary: Prior work in motion generation and world modeling either relied on specialized skeleton parameters or used pixel and point representations that lacked rotation. WMM abstracts entities into rigid SE(3) tokens and uniquely generalizes the Diffusion Forcing concept across both space and time.
sections.details:
### Motion Generation and 4D World Modeling
Previous motion generation models remained fragmented across actor types, such as human bodies (SMPL), hands (MANO), or specific robot platforms. While recent efforts employ LLMs to unify human motion (e.g., MAGNet, UMO), they remain confined to human kinematics.
Conversely, approaches spanning heterogeneous actors (e.g., MoMap, PointWorld, TraceGen) relied on pixel-level 3D point tracking or dense flow. However, these methods only model translation ($\mathbb{R}^3$), discarding the rigid-body rotations and entity identities central to contact and articulated movement. While works like SE3-Nets and SPOT handled rigid transformations, they were restricted to single robots or fixed objects. WMM unifies these paradigms by treating human joints, robot links, and objects alike as sparse SE(3) tokens possessing both rotation and translation, realizing a truly cross-category world model.

### Flexible Policies and Sequence Modeling
Approaches combining world models and policies, such as DreamerV3 and video action models, are tied to specific robot morphologies or raw pixel spaces. For flexible conditioning, Diffusion Forcing—which assigns token-specific noise schedules—is the closest prior work. However, Diffusion Forcing focused primarily along the temporal axis. WMM generalizes this concept across both time and space (entities), and makes it practical for large grids exceeding 10,000 spatiotemporal tokens through factored attention architectures.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Outlook: Toward a Foundation Model for All Dynamic Elements
sections.summary: Using sparse SE(3) trajectories as a shared language alongside flow-matching with per-token noise, WMM acts as a unified generative prior for 4D dynamic worlds. Future work will explore training a single checkpoint across all domains and enabling direct inference from raw RGB video.
sections.details:
This paper introduced World Motion Models (WMMs), a world model grounded on sparse SE(3) pose trajectories as a minimal yet expressive 4D primitive. Combining flow-matching with per-token noise schedules and a context token mechanism, a single set of trained weights executes policies, forward dynamics, inverse dynamics, infilling, and retargeting at state-of-the-art levels by simply swapping inference masks.

The authors also outline several limitations and future research avenues:
First, this work trained separate model checkpoints for each benchmark; pretraining a single large-scale model across all combined domains remains an open step.
Second, because WMM assumes rigid motion (SE(3)), extending the representation to handle general linear and non-linear deformations, such as cloth stretching or fluid flow, will be necessary.
Third, the current pipeline requires pre-estimated depth or geometric states as inputs; enabling end-to-end direct inference from raw RGB video is an important future goal.
Fourth, the model cannot generalize zero-shot to completely unseen kinematic morphologies that were absent during training, motivating deeper investigation into in-context learning via context tokens.

sections.heading: Appendix: Rotation Scaling Justification and Data Generation Pipeline
sections.summary: The appendix evaluates the rationale behind the rotation scaling factor $\delta=0.2$ in pose tokens and ablates geometric and semantic features. It also details the procedure and cost of automatically extracting 3D pose trajectory annotations from standard RGB video using local Procrustes analysis.
sections.details:
### Impact of Rotation Scaling $\delta$
In the 9D pose vector $[\mathbf{x}, \delta \mathbf{r}_1, \delta \mathbf{r}_2]$, the rotation scaling factor $\delta$ is empirically set to $\delta=0.2$ so that the initial flow/diffusion signals align closely with a standard normal distribution (zero mean, unit variance). Ablations on humanoid robot retargeting showed that increasing $\delta$ to $0.6$ or $1.0$ degraded tracking error and simulation success rates, confirming that $\delta=0.2$ achieves the best numerical balance.

### Feature Ablations and Consistency with Parametric Models
On Language Table, zeroing out geometric features $F_{\text{geo}}$ extracted from local point clouds caused a sharp drop in success rate, showing that geometry is vital for language instructions to identify which block to manipulate. On TraceGen, removing DINO semantic features $F_{\text{sem}}$ worsened trajectory error. Furthermore, when projecting predicted SE(3) trajectories onto SMPL or robot joint angles, deviations between raw predictions and kinematically constrained poses (such as off-axis deformations) were minimal, indicating the model naturally respects physical joint constraints.

### Annotation Costs from In-the-Wild Video
To extract training data from standard RGB videos lacking human or URDF models, the pipeline first generates dense 3D point tracking (40 frames, ~32k tracks) and constructs neighborhood topologies based on maximum inter-trajectory distance during co-visible intervals. Solving local rigid transformations via closed-form Procrustes analysis allows rapid, automatic derivation of SE(3) coordinate frame trajectories.

takeaways: All dynamic elements in 4D scenes—including humans, objects, robot joints, and cameras—can be unified under the shared language of sparse SE(3) trajectories.
Training flow-matching with independent noise levels across all spatiotemporal tokens enables a single model to act as a policy, world model, or planner simply by altering inference masks.
Providing distant goals or cross-embodiment demonstrations as out-of-sequence context tokens enables non-causal inference and cross-embodiment learning with minimal complexity.
Setting known tokens to a small non-zero noise level (e.g., 0.05) instead of 0 provides robustness against observation noise by allowing the model to self-correct sensor jitter during generation.
limitations: Separate model checkpoints were trained for each benchmark; pretraining a single, massive model spanning all tasks and domains remains unaddressed.
Because it assumes rigid-body motion (SE(3)), direct modeling of non-rigid deformations like stretching cloth or fluids is currently out of scope.
The framework requires estimated depth or geometric states as inputs, rather than running end-to-end directly from monocular RGB video.
Zero-shot generalization to completely unfamiliar skeletal structures or morphologies unseen during training remains challenging.
